content: The Longleaf Pine (Pinus palustris) is a species of pine tree native to the southeastern United States, primarily found along the coastal plain from eastern Texas to southeastern Virginia, extending into northern and central Florida. Its bark is thick, reddish-brown, and scaly. The leaves are dark green, needle-like, and grow in bundles of three. These needles are often twisted and exceptionally long, measuring 20–45 cm (8–18 inches) in length. Among southern pines with long needles, the Longleaf Pine is one of the two species, the other being the Slash Pine. The cones of the Longleaf Pine include both male pollen cones (staminate strobili) and female seed cones (ovulate strobili). These cones begin forming during the growing season before the buds emerge. Male pollen cones start developing in July, while female seed conelets form over a short period in August. Pollination occurs early the following spring, with male cones measuring 3–8 cm (1–3 inches) in length. Female seed cones mature approximately 20 months after pollination. When mature, these cones are yellow-brown, 15–25 cm (6–10 inches) long, and 5–7 cm (2–2.5 inches) wide, opening to a width of 12 cm (5 inches). Each scale of the cone has a small but sharp downward-pointing spine. The seeds are 7–9 mm long, with a wing measuring 25–40 mm (1–1.75 inches). The Longleaf Pine takes 100 to 150 years to reach full size and can live up to 300 years. In its early stages, it develops a long taproot, typically 2–3 meters (6–10 feet) in length. As the tree matures, it forms a wide-spreading lateral root system with several deep sinker roots. This species thrives on well-drained, sandy soils, often forming pure stands. In northern Alabama, it can also grow on clay soils. The scientific name palustris, meaning of marshes, is a misnomer attributed to Philip Miller, who mistakenly associated the species with marshy areas due to observing temporary winter flooding in Longleaf Pine forests. The Longleaf Pine is also known as Southern Yellow Pine or Longleaf Yellow Pine. Historically, it was referred to as Pitch Pine, but this name was abandoned to avoid confusion with another species, Pinus rigida. Longleaf Pines are commonly found in upland pine forest habitats. Ecologically, the Longleaf Pine is highly resistant to fire. Periodic natural wildfires favor this species by eliminating competing trees, resulting in open Longleaf Pine forests or savannas. Young seedlings do not resemble typical trees but instead appear as a green fountain of needles, a stage known as the grass stage. During this stage, which lasts 5–12 years, vertical growth is minimal, and the tree may take years to grow ankle-high. However, once the grass stage ends, the tree undergoes a growth spurt, especially in the absence of a canopy above it. In the grass stage, the tree is highly resistant to grass fires, as the tightly packed needle bases protect the bud from fire damage. Despite this fire resistance, young Longleaf Pines are vulnerable to feral hogs, which contributed significantly to the species' decline when early settlers released swine into woodlands for foraging. Longleaf Pine forests are rich in biodiversity. The endangered Red-cockaded Woodpecker depends on these forests for habitat. The seeds of the Longleaf Pine are large and nutritious, serving as an important food source for birds, such as the Brown-headed Nuthatch, and other wildlife. The U.S. Forest Service is conducting prescribed burning programs in areas like the Francis Marion National Forest near Charleston, South Carolina, to restore Longleaf Pine forests. These efforts aim to increase the forested area to 44,700 acres (180 km²) within ten years and 53,500 acres (217 km²) in the long term. Prescribed burns also enhance the habitat for the Red-cockaded Woodpecker, support wildlife dependent on grass-shrub habitats, and reduce the risk of destructive wildfires. The Red Hills Region of Florida and Georgia contains some of the best-preserved Longleaf Pine stands, maintained through regular burning to promote quail habitat on private hunting plantations. Historically, vast forests of Longleaf Pine stretched along the southeastern Atlantic and Gulf coasts of North America. These forests were a critical source of naval stores, including resin, turpentine, and timber, essential for shipbuilding. Over time, these forests were extensively logged for timber and replaced with faster-growing species like Loblolly Pine and Slash Pine, as well as for agriculture and urban development. As a result, only about 3% of the original Longleaf Pine forests remain, with little new planting occurring. However, the species is available at nurseries within its range, with the southernmost known point of sale in Lake Worth, Florida. The yellow, resinous wood of the Longleaf Pine is used for lumber and pulp. Boards cut from virgin timber in the past were exceptionally wide, up to 1 meter (3 feet), and are now salvaged from demolition projects for reuse as flooring in upscale homes. The stumps and taproots of old trees are saturated with resin and resistant to decay. Farmers often find buried stumps in fields, even in areas cleared a century ago. These stumps are dug up and sold as fat lighter or lighter wood, which is highly sought after as kindling for fireplaces, wood stoves, and barbecue pits. In old-growth pines, the heartwood of the trunk is similarly resin-saturated. Boards cut from this fat lighter wood are heavy, resistant to rot, but highly flammable, making buildings constructed from them prone to intense fires. The Longleaf Pine is the official state tree of Alabama. In North Carolina, the pine tree is the state tree, with the Longleaf Pine specifically celebrated in the official state toast. Before European settlement, Longleaf Pine forests dominated approximately 90 million acres (360,000 km²) from Virginia to Florida and west to eastern Texas. These forests were shaped by frequent widespread fires, which allowed the Longleaf Pine to remain the dominant species. Today, less than 5% of this ecosystem remains. A significant factor in the decline of Longleaf Pine habitat has been the aggressive suppression of necessary fires. Efforts are underway to restore Longleaf Pine ecosystems within their natural range. Organizations like the Longleaf Alliance actively promote research, education, and management of this species.
